company.name: Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence

profile_text.body:
Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence, also known as Stanford HAI, is a non-profit university lab founded in 2019 and based at Stanford, California. Its site states that its mission is to advance humanity through AI and data science, with work focused on discovery, technological innovation, educational transformation, and societal impact. The institute describes its vision as studying, guiding, and developing human-centered AI technologies and applications, and says AI should be collaborative, augmentative, and enhancing of human productivity and quality of life. Fei-Fei Li is named as founding director and senior fellow, and James Landay as Denning director.

Per its own site, HAI runs courses for leaders and decision-makers on AI technologies and their business implications, specialized training programs for policymakers and civil servants, and education work aimed at the K-12 ecosystem, teachers, and students. It offers fellowship and grant programs, affinity groups for students, and policy work it describes as evidence-based research and global convenings. Research and commentary highlighted on the site include a study finding that benchmarks often do not measure what they claim, a Prompt Response series with Surya Ganguli, Diyi Yang, and Rob Reich on emergent agent behavior, recursive self-improvement, independent evaluation, and whether a kill switch can make advanced AI safer, work by policy fellow Jennifer King on AI privacy, a response by James Landay to AI doomerism, work on governance for AI in clinical settings, and a piece by Caroline Meinhardt, Thomas Mullaney, Juan N. Pava, and Diyi Yang noting that over 6,000 of the world's 7,000-plus living languages remain digitally disadvantaged.

The institute's recorded aliases include Stanford HAI, Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI, HAI, and AI Index. No products, MCP servers, or lawsuits are listed for it. Its law exposure is recorded in California, with no individual cases named.
